flashcards.q: Why does per-seat pricing specifically break down for AI agents that substitute human labor?
flashcards.a: Per-seat pricing assumes value scales with headcount. A good AI agent reduces the number of humans needed, so a vendor pricing per seat is financially rewarded when their own product under-delivers -- the customer keeps (and pays for) more seats precisely because the AI isn't good enough to replace the work.

flashcards.q: What is the alignment gap in usage-based pricing for AI products specifically?
flashcards.a: Usage is a proxy for consumption, not value delivered -- a poorly-performing AI assistant needing 5 retries to get a correct answer generates 5x the revenue of a well-performing one, for delivering LESS value, not more.

flashcards.q: What's the biggest design risk in outcome-based AI pricing (e.g. charging per resolved support ticket)?
flashcards.a: Goodhart's Law baked into the pricing CONTRACT itself: a vague or gameable definition of 'outcome' creates a direct financial incentive to mark things resolved that aren't actually resolved -- more dangerous than an internal KPI being gamed because it's now commercial, not just organizational.

flashcards.q: What mitigations make an outcome-based pricing definition harder to game?
flashcards.a: A reopened-item clawback (credit/reversal if a 'resolved' ticket reopens within N days), customer confirmation of resolution, and independent audit sampling of billed outcomes against actual transcripts -- guardrails need independence from the party being paid based on the metric.

flashcards.q: Why has hybrid pricing (base fee + usage/outcome component) become the majority pattern for AI products?
flashcards.a: Pure usage-based pricing creates unpredictable bills enterprise procurement dislikes; pure outcome-based pricing requires a verifiable outcome definition many use cases don't have yet, and puts all demand-volatility risk on the vendor. A base fee gives predictability, the variable component gives incentive alignment -- Stripe data found hybrid associated with higher median growth than either pure model.

flashcards.q: What percentage of enterprise AI projects were approved on projected ROI that was never actually measured after launch?
flashcards.a: 61% (per 2025 MIT Sloan research) -- the project shipped and nobody checked whether the projected value materialized. This is a process failure, not a model-capability failure.

flashcards.q: What's the success-rate difference between AI projects with a quantified success metric defined upfront versus those without?
flashcards.a: Roughly 54% success rate with a defined metric upfront, versus roughly 12% without -- a 4-5x difference attributable to one specific, cheap, process-level practice. 73% of FAILED AI projects had no agreed success definition before starting.

flashcards.q: What percentage of organizations see measurable P&L return from their generative AI pilots, per 2025 MIT Sloan research?
flashcards.a: Only about 5% capture value at scale -- 95% see no measurable P&L return. The data attributes this overwhelmingly to undefined success criteria and unmeasured post-launch outcomes, not primarily to model capability failure.

flashcards.q: What connects the strategy module's 'AI wrapper is not a moat' point to real market outcomes?
flashcards.a: AI wrapper startups show roughly 80% failure rates, with 60-70% generating zero revenue ever -- the empirical outcome of lacking process power, switching costs, or a cornered resource: a fast-follower or the foundation-model provider itself can replicate the visible value proposition faster than the wrapper company can build a durable position.

flashcards.q: What did the 2026 buyer survey find about pricing model preference, and what does it mean for seat-only vendors?
flashcards.a: 43% of buyers prefer consumption-based pricing, 27% favor outcome-based. Seat-only vendors are increasingly disqualified from AI-product deals before they even reach a demo -- buyers have absorbed the 'seat pricing rewards under-delivery' argument.
